about.build: the 0.7.0 PGO release build: the binaries of the GitHub release assets nanocodec-0.7.0-x86_64-linux and -aarch64-linux (commit ce89975ea; tools/dev/pgo_build.sh: profile-guided, trained by encoding public clips with every shipped preset and decoding the streams; fat LTO, one codegen unit, x86-64-v3 code generation on x86); the decoders' SIMD kernels are chosen at run time (AVX-512 on Granite Rapids, NEON and SVE2 on Graviton 4)
about.browser_build: the v0.7.0 browser module (tools/web/build.sh, its relaxed-SIMD build: SIMD128 plus relaxed SIMD)
about.method: Each process reads its stream into memory, then decodes it 3 times, each pass with a fresh one-thread decoder and frames discarded; neither side is charged process start-up, probing, demuxing or output. 5 interleaved rounds (order reversed every other round): 15 passes per decoder and stream; the figure is the median pass.
about.harnesses: ours: nanocodec decode --bench; FFmpeg and dav1d: libavcodec-bench (tools/anchors/libavcodec_bench.c, packets demuxed by libavformat before timing); libvpx, VVdeC, AVM and dav2d: vpx-bench, vvdec-bench, avm-bench, dav2d-bench (tools/anchors/*_bench.c), each against its pinned static library, units split in memory before timing.
about.browser_method: tools/web/ffmpeg_wasm_yardstick.py under node (V8), one process per run, 7 interleaved rounds: ours the BrowserDecoder.decode calls (the display hand-off, I420 to RGBA, is not included), ffmpeg.wasm the sum of its decode_video calls as -benchmark_all logs them; neither is charged module start-up, probing or demuxing. The earlier 13-stream browser table (<machine>/yardstick.json, the first session) is kept in the record; the page now shows the all-stream WebAssembly comparison, timed in a third session; the native column beside it is the PGO build's.
about.ffmpeg_wasm: @ffmpeg/core 0.12.10, the official single-thread build: FFmpeg 5.1.4 under emscripten with --disable-asm and -O3 -msimd128 (compiler-generated SIMD128 only, FFmpeg's hand-written SIMD kernels off); it has no AV1, VVC or AV2 decoder
about.streams: Two stream sets. Benchmark streams: 7 clips of the BP-4 "ours" held-out set (one per content class; 960x540 to 1280x720, 600 frames, the 1200 kbps rung), each coded by our six encoders at Medium and by x264 medium, x265 medium, libvpx VP9 rt 7, SVT-AV1 M10 and libaom rt 8 (the benchmark's streams). Earlier yardstick streams (2026-11-23): 720p to 4K, among them camera recordings (Axis, Hanwha, a Novatek bodycam) and streams from x264, x265, openh264, SVT-AV1, libaom and libvpx. Our streams come from development builds; only the decoders are 0.7.0's.
about.plain_build: Beside it, in the same rounds: the plain release build of the same commit (no PGO, as crates.io builds it), the page's secondary column
about.wasm_yardsticks: Every stream of the native comparison that each yardstick decodes, under node v22.21.1 (V8) on the same machine, one core per process: tools/web/wasm_yardsticks.py, 5 interleaved rounds (order reversed every other round), one process per run. Each process decodes the stream twice, a fresh decoder each pass, and the faster pass counts (WebAssembly starts in V8's baseline compiler); the official ffmpeg.wasm runs one command per module and has one pass. As natively, only the decode calls are timed: no module start-up, demuxing or output. The figure is the median over the rounds. Our module is the v0.7.0 relaxed-SIMD build (the same file, by hash, as the browser runs before), re-timed in these rounds.
about.wasm_builds: The WebAssembly yardsticks were built by us (tools/web/build_wasm_yardsticks.sh; emscripten 4.0.10, -O3 -msimd128, no threads; every flag in wasm-build-flags.json): FFmpeg n8.0.1 (its h264, hevc, vvc and vp9 decoders; configured for --arch=wasm with its simd128 extension, so its only hand-written WebAssembly SIMD kernels, HEVC's inverse transforms and SAO filters, are on; all else is C vectorised by the compiler), dav1d 1.5.4 (its C code: dav1d has no WebAssembly kernels; through libavcodec, as natively) and libvpx v1.16.0 (its generic C target: no WebAssembly kernels upstream). Each is timed by the native comparison's own in-process harness (tools/anchors/libavcodec_bench.c, vpx_bench.c) compiled with it.
about.webcodecs: Chrome's own decoders are native code with their assembly (FFmpeg for H.264, libvpx for VP9, dav1d for AV1) or the GPU's decoder, not WebAssembly, and a web page cannot ship them: a different kind of yardstick from the WebAssembly ones above. Timed in the same headless Chrome as our module (tools/web/webcodecs_yardstick.py), one fresh page per run, the whole browser bound to one core with taskset (Chrome's decoder threads share it): a VideoDecoder over every chunk of the stream, all queued at once, from the first decode() to flush() resolving, each frame closed on output and never read back; our module, the BrowserDecoder.decode calls. Both the faster of two passes per page, median over interleaved rounds (5 on AWS, 2 on the PC). 'prefer-hardware' fails rather than falls back to software, so a stream it decodes was decoded by the platform decoder. Chrome on Linux has no software HEVC decoder, and WebCodecs has no codec string for VVC or AV2. On the PC, hardware decode is the RTX 5090's NVDEC through VA-API (nvidia-vaapi-driver 0.0.14): Chrome needs a window for it (headless Chrome cannot set up the decoder's output), so the PC run's Chrome drew into a private headless Wayland compositor (gnome-shell --headless), not onto any display. The GPU was shared with other work during the run.

c8i.name: c8i.2xlarge (Intel Granite Rapids)
c8i.anchors: Each built from its pinned source without -march, keeping its own run-time ISA dispatch (AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels where it has them).

c8g.label: Arm (Graviton 4)
c8g.name: c8g.2xlarge (Graviton 4)
c8g.anchors: Each built from its pinned source for generic aarch64 (on the project's Jetson, without -march), with its NEON assembly and its own run-time dispatch; none was built with Graviton 4 specific options.
